title: Complete Transition Reference — All Figma Prototype Animations
content:
INSTANT — the destination replaces the source immediately. No settings. Correct for genuinely discontinuous jumps and for grey-box flow testing. Wrong as a default, because it strips all spatial meaning.

DISSOLVE — cross-fade the destination in over the source. Settings: duration, easing. Correct when there is no spatial relationship between the two states: a theme change, a completely different screen, a mode switch. Wrong for anything the user should read as 'the same thing, moved'.

SMART ANIMATE — Figma finds layers matching by name and hierarchy across the two frames and interpolates their differences. Settings: duration, easing. This is the only transition that expresses continuity of object identity.

MOVE IN / MOVE OUT — the destination slides in over (Move in) or the source slides out revealing (Move out) the destination. Settings: direction (left, right, top, bottom), easing, duration. Move in is the classic push-a-modal-up-from-the-bottom.

PUSH — the destination pushes the source out of frame; both move together, like a filmstrip. Settings: direction, easing, duration. Correct for peer-level lateral navigation: tabs, carousel steps, onboarding pages.

SLIDE IN / SLIDE OUT — like Move, but the outgoing frame offsets slightly rather than staying still, producing a subtler parallax. Settings: direction, easing, duration.

SMART ANIMATE MATCHING LAYERS — a hybrid checkbox on Move/Push/Slide. Matching layers smart-animate; non-matching layers use the primary transition. Fixed layers that match get NO transition; fixed layers that don't match dissolve.

title: Which Transition Means What
content:
Transitions are grammar, not decoration. Each one makes a claim about the relationship between two states.

'THIS IS THE SAME OBJECT, CHANGED' → Smart animate. A card expanding into a detail view, a thumbnail becoming a hero image, a collapsed row opening, a number counting up.

'THIS IS A SIBLING, BESIDE THE LAST ONE' → Push. Tabs, carousel slides, onboarding steps, month-to-month in a calendar. Direction encodes order: forward pushes left, back pushes right (in LTR).

'THIS IS A LAYER ON TOP' → Move in from bottom (sheets, mobile modals) or Dissolve with an overlay (dialogs). The source must remain visible underneath, which means overlay, not navigate.

'THIS IS SOMEWHERE ELSE ENTIRELY' → Dissolve, or Instant. Switching from the storefront to the admin, from light to dark theme, from one product to an unrelated one.

'THIS IS DEEPER IN' → Move in from right (LTR) with the source staying put, or Smart animate if a shared element carries the continuity. Coming back reverses the direction — always.

DIRECTIONAL CONSISTENCY IS NON-NEGOTIABLE. If forward is right-to-left, backward must be left-to-right, everywhere, with no exceptions. Inconsistent direction is the fastest way to make a product feel unreliable, and users notice it without being able to name it.

THE TEST: describe the transition in words. If the sentence is 'it fades because I didn't pick anything', go back and pick.

title: Smart Animate — How Matching Actually Works
content:
Smart animate interpolates between two frames by finding MATCHING LAYERS. Figma matches on two criteria simultaneously: LAYER NAME and POSITION IN THE HIERARCHY. Both must correspond.

CONSEQUENCES:
- 'Rectangle 12' in frame A matches 'Rectangle 12' in frame B only if it sits at the same place in the tree. Same name at a different depth does not match.
- Duplicating the frame (Cmd/Ctrl+D) is the reliable way to start, because it guarantees identical names and identical hierarchy. Then change only what should animate.
- Copy-pasting a layer between frames preserves its name, so 'Rectangle 1' pasted into another frame is still 'Rectangle 1' and will match.
- Renaming a layer in one frame silently breaks the match, and Figma falls back to dissolve for that layer without warning.

VERIFY, DON'T GUESS: in the Prototype tab, hover a layer to preview which layers Figma considers matching across the connection. Do this before debugging by trial and error — it turns a twenty-minute guessing game into a five-second check.

DELIBERATE NON-MATCHING: give layers unique names when you want them to fade rather than fly. Two unrelated cards both named 'Card' at the same hierarchy level will morph into each other in a way that looks like a bug. Name them 'card / featured' and 'card / recent' and they dissolve independently.

HIERARCHY FOR LAYERING: matching layers should sit near the top of the hierarchy when combined with Move or Slide, or the incoming frame will render over the element that is supposed to be flying.
source: help.figma.com — Smart animate layers between frames

title: Smart Animate — Supported and Unsupported Properties
content:
ANIMATES:
- SCALE — width and height changes. Objects grow and shrink smoothly.
- POSITION — X and Y. This is the fly-across-the-screen behaviour.
- OPACITY — set the LAYER opacity to 0%, not the visibility toggle. Toggling visibility (the eye icon) makes the layer absent, which is not the same as transparent, and produces a pop instead of a fade.
- ROTATION.
- FILL — solid colour, gradient, and image fills interpolate.
- CORNER RADIUS interpolates as part of shape properties.

DOES NOT ANIMATE (falls back to dissolve for the affected layer):
- DROP SHADOW and INNER SHADOW. This is the most-hit limitation. An elevation change on a card cannot smart-animate; the shadow pops. Workaround: put the shadow on a separate matching rectangle behind the card and animate its opacity, or accept the pop.
- SHAPE MORPHING between different shape types. A rectangle cannot become an ellipse; a vector cannot become a different vector. Workaround: cross-fade two shapes stacked on each other.
- OVERLAY actions. Open overlay cannot use Smart animate at all. Overlay-to-overlay SWAPS can, if the overlays share matching layers.
- STROKE WEIGHT and stroke properties animate unreliably; test before relying on them.

PARTIAL: texture, noise, background blur, and layer blur do animate, but reliably only when the frames were duplicated from each other.

WHEN SMART ANIMATE FALLS BACK: names don't match, hierarchy differs, an unsupported property changed, or the layer is new in the destination. Figma applies a default dissolve and says nothing.
source: help.figma.com — Smart animate layers between frames

title: Easing Presets — All Eight Bezier Curves
content:
Figma's easing dropdown, in order of when to reach for them.

LINEAR — constant speed. Mechanical and lifeless for anything with mass. The ONLY correct uses are continuous loops: progress bars, spinners, shimmer, marquees.

EASE OUT — fast start, decelerating finish. The workhorse. Use for anything ENTERING: menus opening, modals arriving, tooltips appearing, content loading in. It reads as something arriving and settling.

EASE IN — slow start, accelerating finish. Use for anything LEAVING: dismissals, deletions, exits. It reads as something departing and gathering speed off-screen. Using ease-in on an entrance is the most common easing mistake — it makes the element feel reluctant.

EASE IN AND OUT — slow, fast, slow. Use for movement BETWEEN two on-screen positions, where both departure and arrival are visible: a card repositioning, a slider handle moving, a scroll-to.

EASE IN BACK — anticipates by overshooting backwards before moving. Use for a windup: a button that dips before launching something.

EASE OUT BACK — overshoots the target then settles. Use for arrivals that should feel confident or playful: a toast landing, an icon popping in, an added-to-cart badge.

EASE IN AND OUT BACK — anticipation plus overshoot. Rarely correct; it draws attention to the animation rather than the content.

CUSTOM BEZIER — four control points on a graph. Reach for it when you have a motion token from engineering (e.g. cubic-bezier(0.2, 0, 0, 1)) and need the prototype to match the build exactly.
source: help.figma.com — Prototype easing and spring animations

title: Spring Animations — Presets and Custom Physics
content:
Springs are physics-based rather than curve-based: the animation runs until the spring settles, so duration is emergent rather than set.

PRESETS:
- GENTLE — slow, soft spring with minimal overshoot. The neutral choice. Good for scaling content, expanding panels, anything that should feel calm.
- QUICK — a bit more spring, fast settle. Good for toasts, notifications, snackbars, chips.
- BOUNCY — high energy, noticeable overshoot and oscillation before settling. Good for a single delightful moment — a heart animating on like, a reward badge. Ruinous if used more than once per screen.
- SLOW — steady with a long settle and minimal overshoot. Good for scaling up full-screen content, hero reveals.
- CUSTOM — three parameters.

CUSTOM PARAMETERS:
- STIFFNESS — controls the frequency of the bounce. Higher is faster and tighter.
- DAMPING — controls how quickly oscillation dies. Higher damping means less bounce; low damping wobbles.
- MASS — affects speed and bounce height. Heavier is slower and travels further past the target.

You can drag the animated graph to adjust stiffness and damping; mass is entered numerically. You can extend the curve beyond the graph's dashed perimeter to create an anticipatory dip at the start or a rebound at the end.

LIMITATIONS AND HANDOFF: custom curves cannot be saved as a reusable style, but the numeric values can be copied and pasted between interactions. Keep your spring values in a written motion spec — 'bouncy' is not implementable, 'stiffness 320 / damping 22 / mass 1' is. Note that Figma's spring maths and a given code library's spring maths are not identical; expect to tune once in code.
source: help.figma.com — Prototype easing and spring animations

title: Duration — Numbers That Actually Work
content:
Figma's duration field is in milliseconds. Defaults are a starting point, not a decision.

THE SCALE:
- 0ms — instant. State changes with no spatial meaning.
- 50–100ms — micro. Button press, toggle flip, checkbox tick, hover colour. At this length the user perceives responsiveness, not motion.
- 150–250ms — short. Tooltips, dropdowns, chips, small fades, focus rings, accordion rows. This is where most UI motion belongs.
- 250–400ms — medium. Modals, sheets, panel slides, page transitions, expanding cards. 300ms is the single most useful default.
- 400–700ms — long. Multi-element choreography, hero reveals, onboarding sequences. Justify every one of these.
- Over 700ms — almost always wrong in product UI. The user has finished reading and is waiting for your animation.

RULES:
- Larger travel distance needs slightly more time, but sub-linearly. Doubling the distance does not double the duration.
- Exits should be FASTER than entrances, typically 60–75% of the entrance duration. Users want dismissal to feel immediate; they will tolerate an arrival taking its time.
- Repeated actions must be short. If a user will do it fifty times an hour, cap it at 150ms.
- While building, temporarily raise the duration to 1000ms+ so you can see what Smart animate is actually doing, then set it back. Figma's docs recommend exactly this.

THE HONEST TEST: play the transition ten times in a row. Anything that starts to annoy you on the third pass is too long.

title: Smart Animate Recipes — Common Effects
content:
EXPAND CARD TO DETAIL. Duplicate the frame. In the destination, resize the card to fill, move the image to hero position, add the detail content. Every shared layer keeps its name. Smart animate, 350ms, ease-out. The unshared detail content is new in the destination, so it dissolves in — stagger the feel by making it a single group that fades.

ACCORDION OPEN. Two frames or two variants. In the open state, the content frame has real height and the chevron is rotated 180°. Smart animate, 250ms, ease-out. Auto layout on the parent means everything below reflows automatically — which Smart animate then animates for free.

TAB SWITCH WITH SLIDING INDICATOR. The indicator is one layer with the same name in both frames, at different X positions. Smart animate, 200ms, ease-in-out. The panel content beneath should be a differently-named group per tab so it cross-fades rather than morphing.

NUMBER COUNTING UP. Two text layers with the same name, different values. Smart animate does not interpolate text content — it cross-fades. For a genuine count, bind a number variable to the text and increment it, or use Figma Motion.

BOTTOM SHEET DRAG. Overlay positioned Bottom centre. Two overlay states (peek and full) with matching layers, connected with On drag Up / On drag Down and Smart animate. Because drag is bidirectional the sheet follows the finger.

PROGRESS BAR FILL. One rectangle, same name, different width across frames. Smart animate with LINEAR easing — this is one of the few correct uses of linear.

SKELETON TO CONTENT. Skeleton frame and content frame where the skeleton blocks and the real elements share names and positions. Smart animate, 300ms, ease-out, triggered After delay. Reads as content resolving in place rather than replacing the page.

title: Debugging a Transition That Won't Animate
content:
SYMPTOM: it dissolves instead of animating.
CAUSES, in the order to check them —
1. Layer names differ between frames. Check spelling, trailing spaces, and casing.
2. Hierarchy differs. The layer is nested one level deeper in one frame, often because you accidentally grouped it.
3. An unsupported property changed — most often a shadow. Isolate by reverting the shadow and testing again.
4. The layer is new in the destination and has nothing to animate from.
5. You are on an Open overlay action, which cannot smart-animate at all.
VERIFY: hover the layer in the Prototype tab to see Figma's matching preview.

SYMPTOM: the wrong things fly across the screen.
CAUSE: two unrelated layers share a name at the same hierarchy level. Give them distinct names.

SYMPTOM: the element animates but renders behind something.
CAUSE: hierarchy order. Matching layers need to be near the top of the tree when combined with Move/Slide/Push.

SYMPTOM: it works on canvas but not in Presentation view.
CAUSES: interaction is on an instance override that Presentation view ignores; or the destination is not a top-level frame; or a layer above is swallowing the click.

SYMPTOM: it looks janky.
CAUSES: too many matching layers (hundreds), heavy blur or shadow on the animating frames, or large raster images being scaled. Reduce the count of animating layers.

SYMPTOM: something pops in at the start instead of fading.
CAUSE: you toggled layer visibility instead of setting layer opacity to 0%.

title: Motion Restraint — When Not to Animate
content:
The strongest motion decision is usually subtraction.

DO NOT ANIMATE:
- Anything the user does dozens of times per session. Repeated motion becomes friction. A list row that animates on every tap is a 200ms tax fifty times an hour.
- Data updating in place, in any financial or trading context. A price that animates while a user is reading it is a legibility failure and, in crypto, a trust failure — did the number change, or did it animate?
- Error messages. They must appear instantly and stay put. An error that eases in delays the information the user most needs.
- Anything above the fold on first load. Entrance animations on hero content delay the moment of comprehension and interact badly with real-world layout shift.
- Two things at once, unrelated. Simultaneous unrelated motion has no focal point and reads as instability.

ANIMATE WHEN THE MOTION CARRIES INFORMATION:
- Spatial relationship — where did this come from, where did it go.
- Causality — this action produced that result.
- Continuity of identity — this is the same object in a new form.
- State change that is otherwise invisible — a toggle, a save, a sync.
- System status — something is happening and you are not stuck.

THE SUBTRACTION TEST: remove the animation. If the interface is still comprehensible, the animation was decoration. Decoration is legitimate exactly once per surface, on a moment worth celebrating. Beyond that it is cost — build cost, performance cost, and accessibility cost.

title: Choreography — Coordinating Multiple Elements
content:
When several elements move at once, the arrangement matters more than the individual curves.

STAGGER. Related items entering together offset by 30–50ms each. Lead with the most important element. Cap the total sequence at ~500ms — beyond that the last item arrives after the user has moved on. Six list items at 40ms each is 240ms of stagger plus the item duration: acceptable. Twenty items is not; stagger only the first five or six and bring the rest in together.

HIERARCHY OF ATTENTION. One element leads; everything else supports. If two things enter with equal weight, equal duration, and equal emphasis, the user's eye has nowhere to go.

SHARED EASING WITHIN A GROUP. Elements in the same semantic group use the same duration and easing. Mixed curves inside one group read as a rendering bug.

DIRECTIONAL COHERENCE. If content enters from the right, outgoing content exits to the left. Everything in a single transition moves along one consistent axis of motion.

ENTER AND EXIT ARE NOT SYMMETRIC. Reverse the direction, but shorten the exit and switch ease-out to ease-in. A modal that arrives in 300ms ease-out should leave in 200ms ease-in.

INTERRUPTIBILITY. Real interfaces let users cancel mid-flight. Figma cannot express this, so state it in handoff: 'dismissal interrupts and reverses the entrance from its current position, it does not queue behind it.'

IN FIGMA specifically: stagger comes from separate frames chained with After delay, or from Figma Motion's timeline, which is the correct tool the moment you need more than two staggered elements.

title: Motion Expectations by Platform
content:
Motion conventions are platform grammar. Violating them makes a native app feel wrong and a web app feel amateur.

iOS — motion is spatial and springy. Navigation pushes right-to-left with a shared interactive back gesture that follows the finger. Sheets rise from the bottom with a detent system and a rubber-band feel. Durations are short (~300–350ms for navigation). Springs, not bezier curves, are the default idiom. Users expect to be able to interrupt and reverse any transition mid-flight.

ANDROID / MATERIAL 3 — motion is expressive and choreographed, with a documented easing and duration token set (emphasised, standard, and their decelerate/accelerate variants). Container transforms — one surface morphing into another — are the signature pattern, which maps directly to Smart animate on a shared container name. Durations are slightly longer than iOS for large surfaces.

WEB — motion is restrained, because it competes with real page-load behaviour. Keep it under 300ms, keep it to opacity and transform (the only two properties that are cheap to animate), and never animate anything that delays first meaningful paint. Scroll-triggered animation is the main idiom, and it must degrade gracefully.

SHOPIFY STOREFRONTS specifically — motion budget is tight because it trades directly against LCP and CLS, which trade against conversion. Cart drawer slide-in, variant swatch feedback, and add-to-cart confirmation are worth the cost. Hero entrance animations and scroll-reveal on above-the-fold content are not.

CRYPTO / FINTECH — motion should signal system state (pending, confirming, confirmed) and never decorate a number. Transaction states are the one place a longer, deliberate animation earns its keep, because it maps to real elapsed time.
